qs.q: A patient presents with a wrist drop, characterized by unopposed flexion of the hand at the wrist joint. Which nerve is most likely injured?
qs.e: Radial nerve injury paralyzes the extensor muscles of the wrist and digits, resulting in the characteristic wrist drop. The median nerve injury typically results in an 'hand of benediction' or ape hand.
qs.s: Anatomy Marathon 1 — Lower Limb — Revision Guide: MCQs

qs.q: A 28-year-old rock climber presents with pain at the wrist exacerbated by resisted adduction of the hand. Which muscle is primarily responsible for medial deviation at the wrist joint?
qs.e: Flexor carpi ulnaris acts synergistically with extensor carpi ulnaris to produce ulnar deviation of the wrist. Flexor carpi radialis and the radial wrist extensors produce radial deviation.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The wrist joint (radiocarpal and midcarpal joints) links the forearm to the hand, allowing flexion, extension, radial and ulnar deviation. Its complex bony, ligamentous and muscular architecture is essential for hand function and is a frequent site of injury.

sections.p: The wrist consists of two functional joints: the radiocarpal joint (between the radius and the proximal carpal row) and the midcarpal joint (between the proximal and distal carpal rows). Together they provide the hand with a wide range of motion while maintaining stability.
b: Two articulations: radiocarpal and midcarpal
Primary movements: flexion, extension, radial/ulnar deviation

sections.p: The radiocarpal joint is a condyloid joint formed by the distal radius, the articular disc, and the scaphoid, lunate, and triquetrum. The midcarpal joint is a plane joint between the proximal and distal carpal rows.
b: Distal radius and articular disc form the radial side
Scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum articulate with the radius
Capitate and hamate form the ulnar side of the midcarpal joint

sections.p: Volar structures include the flexor tendons and the carpal tunnel; dorsal structures include the extensor tendons and the dorsal sensory branch of the radial nerve.
b: Flexor retinaculum forms the carpal tunnel roof
Extensor retinaculum covers dorsal tendons

sections.p: The radial artery supplies the lateral wrist via the dorsal carpal branch; the ulnar artery supplies the medial side via the palmar carpal branch. Both contribute to the palmar and dorsal carpal arches.
b: Radial artery → dorsal carpal branch
Ulnar artery → palmar carpal branch

sections.p: Sensory innervation comes from the median, ulnar, and radial nerves. Motor fibers to the intrinsic hand muscles travel through the median and ulnar nerves.
b: Median nerve: thenar eminence, lateral palm
Ulnar nerve: medial palm, hypothenar
Radial nerve: dorsal hand sensation

sections.p: The wrist transmits forces from the hand to the forearm and allows precise positioning of the hand for tasks such as gripping, writing, and hammering.
b: Flexion/extension for grip strength
Radial/ulnar deviation for hand alignment

sections.p: Wrist injuries range from fractures (distal radius, scaphoid) to ligamentous sprains and carpal tunnel syndrome. Understanding anatomy guides diagnosis and management.
b: Distal radius fracture: common in falls
Scaphoid fracture: risk of avascular necrosis
Ligament sprain: May cause instability
Carpal tunnel syndrome: Median nerve compression

t.b: Does the image show a fracture or dislocation? Positive fracture confirms bony injury; normal X‑ray with persistent pain suggests occult scaphoid fracture.
Is there bone edema or ligament tear? Detects occult fractures and soft‑tissue injury when X‑ray is negative.
Is median nerve conduction delayed? Confirms carpal tunnel syndrome; normal study suggests alternative diagnosis.

sections.p: Physical exam includes inspection, palpation of bony prominences, range‑of‑motion testing, and specific tests for ligament integrity (e.g., Watson test) and nerve compression (Phalen, Tinel).
b: Pain over scaphoid tubercle after FOOSH suggests scaphoid fracture
Positive Phalen/Tinel indicates median nerve compression
Watson test assesses scapholunate instability

whenToSeekHelp: Severe swelling with loss of sensation in fingers
Progressive deformity or inability to move the wrist

faq.q: Why is the scaphoid prone to avascular necrosis?
faq.a: Its blood supply enters distally; a fracture disrupts flow, risking bone death if not promptly treated.

faq.q: What distinguishes a distal radius fracture from a scaphoid fracture on exam?
faq.a: Distal radius fracture causes dorsal angulation and swelling over the forearm; scaphoid fracture pain is localized to the anatomic snuffbox.

faq.q: When is surgical fixation preferred over casting?
faq.a: When there is displacement >2 mm, intra‑articular involvement, or instability that cannot be maintained in a cast.
